runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its defined GAI risks. Its section 2.4 says that GAI systems raise several privacy risks, and it explains them in three main ways. I read the pages directly because the search tool was unavailable.

**Training data and privacy principles.** Training on large datasets can pull in personal information, which strains core privacy principles. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. The profile also notes a visibility problem: most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

**Leakage and memorization.** Models can expose what they were trained on. The profile describes how during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It calls this data memorization and says it may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

**Inference of personal data.** Models can also work out information they were never given. The profile says GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. Even inaccurate inferences can cause harm: these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them. The profile adds that predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The profile also classifies Data Privacy as a cross-cutting risk. It appears under misuse by humans and under ecosystem or societal risks, and it is linked to jailbreaking-related output controls. Data Privacy; Value Chain and Component Integration; Harmful Bias, and Homogenization are listed among technical/model risks, while Data Privacy; Environmental; Intellectual Property. are listed among ecosystem/societal risks.

I did not find any suggested actions for privacy in the pages I read. Section 2.4 ends before the profile's later action tables, so those may contain additional privacy guidance that I did not check.

The NIST Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its defined GAI risks. Its section 2.4 says that GAI systems raise several privacy risks, and it explains them in three main ways. I read the pages directly because the search tool was unavailable.

**Training data and privacy principles.** Training on large datasets can pull in personal information, which strains core privacy principles. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. The profile also notes a visibility problem: most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

**Leakage and memorization.** Models can expose what they were trained on. The profile describes how during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It calls this data memorization and says it may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

**Inference of personal data.** Models can also work out information they were never given. The profile says GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. Even inaccurate inferences can cause harm: these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them. The profile adds that predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The profile also classifies Data Privacy as a cross-cutting risk. It appears under misuse by humans and under ecosystem or societal risks, and it is linked to jailbreaking-related output controls. Data Privacy; Value Chain and Component Integration; Harmful Bias, and Homogenization are listed among technical/model risks, while Data Privacy; Environmental; Intellectual Property. are listed among ecosystem/societal risks.

I did not find any suggested actions for privacy in the pages I read. Section 2.4 ends before the profile's later action tables, so those may contain additional privacy guidance that I did not check.
